descriptionChirho: Qal stem: to direct one's gaze steadily toward something or someone with attention, interest, or favorable regard. Used of God's regard for Abel's offering (Gen 4:4) versus non-regard for Cain's (Gen 4:5), of people looking to God for help (Isa 17:7-8, 31:1), and of the psalmist's devoted attention to God's statutes (Ps 119:117). Arabic الْتَفَتَ 'turn attention toward,' Korean 돌아보다/바라보다 'look upon/gaze,' Spanish mirar 'to look at,' Hindi देखना 'to see/look.' The core semantic is attentive, purposeful gazing as opposed to casual seeing (cf. ראה).

Qal stem with directional nuance: to turn one's gaze away from something, to avert one's look, to cease regarding. Used in pleas to God to stop scrutinizing the supplicant (Job 7:19, 14:6) and in the imperative command to turn away one's gaze (Isa 22:4). Arabic الْتَفِتْ with directional particle 'turn away,' Korean 돌이키다 'turn back/away,' Spanish apartar la mirada 'avert the gaze,' Hindi दृष्टि फेरना 'turn one's sight.' Distinguished from sense 1 by the privative directional meaning: ceasing to gaze rather than initiating it.

Hiphil stem: causative 'to cause gazing to cease,' i.e. to deliberately avert or withdraw one's gaze from someone. Attested in Ps 39:13 where the psalmist pleads with God to look away (הָשַׁע מִמֶּנִּי) before death. Arabic أَعْرِضْ 'turn away deliberately,' Korean 돌이키소서 'please turn away,' Spanish apartar 'to remove.' The Hiphil adds volitional, causative force compared to the Qal 'look away' sense, emphasizing a deliberate act of withdrawal.

A semantic extension from 'looking about' to 'looking about in panic': to be startled, terrified, or dismayed. Found exclusively in Isa 41:10, 23 in the Hitpael-like form תִּשְׁתָּע (possibly Hithpalel or Pilpel), used as a challenge ('do not be dismayed') and a rhetorical question about the power of idols. Arabic تَرْتَعِبْ 'be terrified,' Korean 놀라다 'be startled,' Spanish desmayarse/asombrarse 'to be dismayed/astonished,' Hindi घबराना 'to be alarmed.' The shift from 'gazing' to 'alarm' parallels similar developments in other Semitic visual verbs.

Of the eyes: to become dim, clouded, or effectively closed -- describing failing vision. Attested in Isa 32:3 (feminine plural תִשְׁעֶינָה referring to עֵינַיִם 'eyes' of those who see). Arabic تَشْخُصُ 'stare blankly,' Korean 감기다 'become closed/sealed,' Spanish cerrarse 'to close,' Hindi अंधी होना 'to become blind.' This sense develops from the core 'gaze' meaning via the idea that gazing becomes impossible -- the faculty of looking is extinguished.
